phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial plosive [b], short open-mid back unrounded vowel [ʊ], and alveolar nasal [n]; the first syllable carries stress.
Voiced postalveolar affricate [dʒ] (like English 'j'), near-close near-front unrounded vowel [ɪ], and alveolar lateral approximant [l].

pronunciation.approximation: 'BUN-jil' — stress the first syllable; the 'j' is the 'j' of 'jump', and the final vowel is short like the 'i' in 'kit'.

pronunciation.note: The name Bunjil is a conventional Latin transcription of an Aboriginal theonym. The PuniCodex restoration capitalises the first letter, giving the standard proper-name form. Because no diacritic or distinctive letter is added, the ASCII string 'bunjil' already encodes the conventional spelling; the name is therefore Tier 2.

domains.title: Creator Eaglehawk
domains.subtitle: Sky Ancestor, Law-Giver, and Moiety Founder
domains.lead: Bunjil is the wedge-tailed eaglehawk made ancestor of the Kulin nations of central Victoria. In the Dreaming he shaped the mountains, rivers, plants, animals, and the laws by which people should live. He is one of two moiety ancestors, paired with Waang the crow, and after his work on earth he was lifted into the sky, where he remains as the star Altair.

cards.name: Creator of Country
cards.desc: He shaped the land, water, flora, and fauna of south-eastern Australia, and established the order of the living world.

cards.name: Sky Ancestor
cards.desc: After creation he ascended to the sky and became the star Altair; his two wives became the black swans beside him.

cards.name: Law-Giver
cards.desc: He gave the Kulin peoples their social and ecological laws, including the obligation to care for Country and each other.

cards.name: Moiety Founder
cards.desc: As the eaglehawk ancestor he heads one of the Kulin moieties, balanced by Waang the crow on the other side.

symbols.name: Wedge-tailed eagle
symbols.meaning: The living form of Bunjil and the largest bird of prey in Australia; a sign of creative power and watchful authority

symbols.name: Spear
symbols.meaning: The instrument with which Bunjil commanded the rising sea to stop, and a mark of law-giving authority

symbols.name: Black swan
symbols.meaning: Bunjil's two wives, who became the stars flanking Altair after his ascent

symbols.name: Rainbow
symbols.meaning: His son Binbeal, the rainbow spirit, who continues the creative lineage

mythology.lead: Bunjil's stories belong to the Dreaming of the Kulin nations, especially the Woiwurrung, Boonwurrung, and Wathaurong peoples. They explain how Country was made, how law was given, and how the creator withdrew into the sky so that he might continue to watch over the world.

myths.title: Shaping the Land and the Law
myths.text: In the Dreaming, Bunjil travelled across what is now central Victoria. He formed the mountains, traced the rivers, named the plants and animals, and laid down the laws that govern how people relate to one another and to Country. These laws are not separate from the land; they are remembered in place names, songlines, and the seasonal responsibilities of each clan. (Massola 1968; Howitt 1904)

myths.title: The Sea That Would Not Stop Rising
myths.text: A Boonwurrung story tells of a time when the Kulin nations fell into conflict, neglecting family and Country. The sea rose in anger and threatened to flood the land. The people went to Bunjil and asked him to intervene. Bunjil agreed, but only if the people would change their ways and respect the law. He walked to the water's edge, raised his spear, and commanded the sea to stop. It did. (Briggs, 'Boon Wurrung Story')

myths.title: Lifted into the Sky
myths.text: When his work on earth was finished, Bunjil gathered his family and asked Waang, who kept the winds in skin bags, to release enough wind to carry them to the sky. Waang opened the whirlwind bag, and the wind lifted Bunjil and his people upward. Bunjil became the bright star Altair; his two wives, the black swans, became the stars on either side. Some accounts say he left this world from the island of Deen Maar. (Howitt 1904; Mudrooroo 1994)

myths.title: Bunjil's Shelter
myths.text: In Gariwerd, the country now known as the Grampians, Bunjil took shelter in a cave in the Black Range. The rock-art site known as Bunjil's Shelter is one of the most important Aboriginal art places in Victoria and remains under the care of Traditional Owners. It is not merely a memory of the ancestor; it is a place where his presence is understood to remain. (Parks Victoria 2009)

syncretism: Bunjil is not a solitary deity but one half of a Kulin social and cosmological pair. The eaglehawk moiety, headed by Bunjil, is balanced by the crow moiety, headed by Waang. This pairing structures kinship, marriage, and ritual obligations across the Kulin nations. Different clans emphasise different episodes — the Woiwurrung stress the sky ascent and Altair, the Boonwurrung remember the rising-sea story, and the Wathaurong preserve place-based accounts tied to the coast and to Bunjil's Shelter. In the colonial period the name was recorded under many spellings — Winjeel, Wingeel, Pundjel, Bunjel — reflecting dialect variation and the difficulty of rendering Aboriginal phonology in English orthography.
culturalLegacy: Bunjil remains a powerful symbol of Aboriginal Victoria. Bunjil's Shelter in the Black Range Scenic Reserve is a protected cultural site and a focus of education and tourism. Public art, including the giant sculpture Eagle in Melbourne, takes Bunjil as its inspiration. For the Wurundjeri, Boonwurrung, and other Kulin communities, Bunjil is not only an ancestral figure but a living authority in discussions of land care, cultural identity, and reconciliation.
extendedMeditation:
Bunjil teaches that creation is not a single event but a continuing responsibility. He did not make the land and depart; he shaped it, gave it law, and then withdrew into the sky so that he could go on watching. The eaglehawk's eye is still understood to be turned toward Country.

For non-Indigenous visitors, Bunjil is an invitation to understand 'Country' not as real estate but as a living inheritance — a place that includes people, animals, plants, water, sky, and story, all held together by obligations that precede the colony. The name Bunjil, even in its simple Latin transcription, carries that whole relationship. To restore the capital is a small act; to remember what it names is the larger one.
originalScriptNote: The Kulin languages were traditionally oral, and Bunjil has no original alphabetic script. The name survives in Latin transcription made by early settlers and anthropologists. PuniCodex therefore treats Bunjil as the scholarly citation form and bunjil as the DNS compromise. The restoration adds only the capital initial; the absence of diacritics or special letters places the name in Tier 2, not because the figure is less significant, but because the ASCII form already carries the conventional spelling.

archaeology: The principal material site associated with Bunjil is Bunjil's Shelter, a rock-art shelter in the Black Range Scenic Reserve within Gariwerd (Grampians National Park region), Victoria. The site is protected under the Aboriginal Heritage Act 2006 and is managed with Traditional Owner input. Textual witnesses include A. W. Howitt's ethnographic notes (AIATSIS MS 69), Aldo Massola's 1968 compilation, and contemporary community publications by Kulin educators and language custodians.

etymology.derivation: Theonym recorded from the Kulin nations of central Victoria, denoting the wedge-tailed eaglehawk creator ancestor. Early colonial collectors produced variant spellings (Winjeel, Wingeel, Pundjel, Bunjel) as they adapted Aboriginal phonology to English orthography.

nameVariations.note: Conventional modern spelling used by Kulin communities, Victorian institutions, and the Aboriginal Heritage Register.
Common alternative spelling reflecting the same pronunciation.
Early colonial spellings recorded by Daniel Bunce and others, now preserved in place names such as Wingeel near Geelong.
Variants appearing in nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century ethnographic literature.
ASCII domain compromise: all lowercase, losing the proper-name capitalisation but retaining the conventional letters.
